\begin{frame}{Advanced Equation Derivations}
  Consider the optimization problem defined as follows:
  \begin{equation}
    \min_{x \in \mathbb{R}^n} f(x) = \frac{1}{2} x^T Q x - c^T x
  \end{equation}
  where $Q \in \mathbb{S}_{++}^n$ is symmetric positive definite.

  \pause

  \begin{align*}
    \nabla f(x) &= Q x - c = 0 \\
    x^* &= Q^{-1} c
  \end{align*}

  The cost at optimal point $x^*$ satisfies:
  $$f(x^*) = -\frac{1}{2} c^T Q^{-1} c < 0.$$
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Theoretical Properties and Proof}
  \begin{block}{Theorem 1 (Convergence Rate)}
    Under the assumption that $\alpha \le \frac{2}{\lambda_{\max}(Q)}$, gradient descent satisfies:
    \begin{equation*}
      \|x_{k+1} - x^*\| \le \rho \|x_k - x^*\|
    \end{equation*}
    with contraction factor $\rho < 1$.
  \end{block}

  \begin{proof}
    Direct expansion of the recursive relation yields:
    $x_{k+1} - x^* = (I - \alpha Q)(x_k - x^*).$
    Taking operator norms on both sides completes the proof.
  \end{proof}
\end{frame}
